title: Atomic type
body:
Individual [[Data type]]

---

An atomic type holds **exactly one value** and has no parts you can reach into. `int`,
`double`, `float`, `char`, `bool`. The name is the course's; "primitive", "built-in", and
"fundamental" mean the same thing, see [[Primitive type]].

The opposite is a [[Compound type]]: [[Array]], [[Structure]], [[C-String]], all of which
hold many values under one name.

| Type | Holds | Typical size | Literal |
|---|---|---|---|
| [[Integer\|int]] | whole numbers | 4 bytes | `42` |
| [[Double\|double]] | real numbers | 8 bytes | `3.14` |
| [[Float\|float]] | real numbers, less precision | 4 bytes | `3.14f` |
| [[Character\|char]] | one character | 1 byte | `'a'` |
| [[Boolean\|bool]] | true or false | 1 byte | `true` |

Sizes are the usual ones, not guarantees; the standard only fixes the minimums, which is
why `sizeof` exists. [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] is where they stop being conventions and
become bit layouts: [[Data representation]], [[Integer Representation]],
[[Boolean Representation]], [[ASCII]].

Two things follow from "holds one value directly":

- Assignment copies the value. Two `int`s are never two names for one number.
- [[Call by value]] gives the function its own copy, so it cannot change yours. Getting
  around that is what [[Call by reference]] is for.

Every [[Variable]] must be declared with a type before it is used, and C++ will not infer
it. Converting between them is [[Type casting]], which is where integer division quietly
truncates and surprises you.
